newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France's Chirac wants Amsterdam budget pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France's Chirac wants Amsterdam budget pact.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday he hoped a stability pact limiting the budget deficits of countries that join a single European currency could be concluded at a summit in Amsterdam next week.

Speaking a day after France's new Socialist-led government requested a delay to study the stability pact, the conservative president said he backed the left-wing administration's drive to get more emphasis on employment in European Union policy.
The French move sparked anger in Germany, which had pressed for the budget discipline accord to reassure its public anxious at abandoning the deutschemark to adopt the euro.
After talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, Chirac said: "France has committed itself to economic and monetary union and is determined that the euro be launched on January 1, 1999.

"That assumes that we examine in Amsterdam the stability and growth pact, which I hope can be concluded in Amsterdam, and also the social measures and economic policy coordination which the French government has rightly just emphasised," he said.

His remarks appeared aimed also at gently forcing the government's hand to accepting a deal at the June 16-17 summit even though Socialist European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici said on Monday he did not believe the French review of the pact could be concluded in time for Amsterdam.
An official in Chirac's office said the president was determined that France should speak with one voice on the issue.

Both Chirac and Kok said they were optimistic that the summit would also be able to conclude negotiations on reforming European Union institutions, which some analysts had suggested might be put at risk because of the row over the stability pact.

Kok sought to address French concerns, telling reporters the French government was not alone in wanting to stress jobs. All EU member states sought a Europe which was not just monetarist but also focused on employment, he said.
"It is important to see how one can develop an additional element on top of the stability pact" to promote jobs, he said.
Kok, current holder of the EU's rotating presidency, said he hoped for "good preparations" on the stability pact before Amsterdam, but he added "there is no guarantee".

European Union leaders negotiated the pact -- which would limit euro-zone countries' public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product after 1999 -- at a summit in Dublin last December but they are due to formally approve it next week.

European Commission president Jacques Santer is due in Paris on Tursday for talks aimed at resolving French concerns over the stability pact, and Chirac and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will meet German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday.
